title: Buuz
description: Steamed lamb dumplings pleated closed with a small vent at the top. A stiff unleavened dough, a fatty filling loosened with water, and about twenty-five minutes of folding.
notes: Lean mince makes a disappointing buuz. You want something around a fifth fat, because the fat melts into the water in the filling and becomes the mouthful of juice that the vent at the top is there to protect.

ingredients.name: onion
ingredients.note: diced as finely as you can manage

steps.text: Work the plain flour, salt and warm water into a stiff dough, then knead it on the bench until the surface goes smooth.
steps.tip: Stiffer than feels right. A soft dough tears open the moment you start pleating it.

steps.text: Cover the dough and leave it to rest at room temperature.
steps.tip: Resting is not a formality here. Unrested gluten springs back as fast as you roll it and you will fight every round.

steps.text: Chop the minced lamb further by hand if it looks pasty, then mix it with the onion, garlic, caraway seeds, salt, black pepper and the water.
steps.tip: Stir in one direction for a full minute. The filling turns tacky and holds itself together while you pleat, instead of sliding out of the round.

steps.text: Roll the dough into a rope, cut it into walnut-sized pieces, and roll each one into a round that is thick in the middle and thin at the rim.
steps.tip: The thick centre is structural. It is the only part carrying the weight of the filling once the buuz is standing up in the steamer.

steps.text: Pleat each round closed around a heaped spoon of filling, leaving a small opening at the very top.
steps.tip: The gap is deliberate. It lets steam out so the dumpling does not split at the side and lose its juice into the tray.

steps.text: Oil the steamer tray, stand the buuz on it without letting them touch, and steam over a hard boil until the dough is glossy and no longer tastes floury.
Let them sit for a minute before anyone picks one up.
steps.tip: Straight out of the steamer the juice inside is hotter than the dumpling looks. One minute is the difference between a good mouthful and a burnt palate.
